title: Real Estate Development and Urban Resilience Under Uncertainty: Coupling Coordination, Regime Switching, and Spatial Spillovers in Guangdong, China
content: This study examines how real estate development shapes urban resilience under uncertainty, using a balanced panel of 21 prefecture-level cities in Guangdong, China, over 2005–2024. Real estate market development (REM) and urban resilience (UR) are measured with entropy-weighted composite indices, and their relationship is examined through coupling coordination analysis, two-way fixed-effects models, a moderating-effect model, a Hansen panel threshold model, and a spatial Durbin model. Four findings emerge. First, the coupling coordination degree rose from 0.233 in 2005 to a peak of 0.397 in 2019 and fell back to 0.280 in 2024, remaining within the imbalanced range throughout, with the Pearl River Delta (0.364) clearly leading the rest of the province. Second, real estate expansion exhibits a significant negative average association with urban resilience (−0.145, p < 0.05). Third, this association is state-dependent: the REM × UNC interaction is significantly positive (+2.130, p < 0.001), and the threshold test identifies an uncertainty threshold of 0.074 below which real estate development weakens resilience (−0.153) and above which it strengthens it (+0.752). Fourth, the spatial Durbin model reveals negative strategic interaction (ρ = −0.974) and a negative spillover from neighbouring real estate expansion (−0.471, p < 0.05), with the moderating mechanism concentrated in the Pearl River Delta. The results imply that the resilience function of the real estate market is a direction-switching function of the uncertainty environment, calling for state-contingent regulation, regionally coordinated governance, and a repositioning of real estate from a growth instrument toward a resilience support system.
